title: Automated Cerebrospinal Fluid Flow Quantification in Hydrocephalus Using Phase-Contrast Magnetic Resonance Imaging

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Automated Cerebrospinal Fluid Flow Quantification in Hydrocephalus Using Phase-Contrast Magnetic Resonance Imaging》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · nbm70431-sec-0001-p3】This study evaluates operator‐dependent variability in C2–C3 CSF segmentation and flow quantification in PC‐MRI, using repeated segmentations from expert and novice operators and comparing them with a fixed automatic DL segmentation pipeline. Specifically, the objective is to assess whether fully repeatable automatic segmentation can provide quantitative CSF flow measurements that are consistent with a multi‐expert reference. The analysis focuses on ROI surface area, flow waveform, peak flow amplitude, and SV, thereby evaluating whether differences in segmentation propagate to clinically relevant hydrodynamic parameters.

【Introduction · nbm70431-sec-0001-p1】Quantitative assessment of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow is clinically relevant in hydrocephalus because altered craniospinal hydrodynamics may reflect changes in intracranial compliance, ventricular‐subarachnoid pressure transmission, and CSF circulation [1, 2, 3, 4]. Phase‐contrast magnetic resonance imaging (PC‐MRI) provides a noninvasive method for encoding CSF velocity over the cardiac cycle and deriving hydrodynamic end‐points, including flow waveforms, peak flow amplitude, and stroke volume (SV) [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. These measurements are used to characterize CSF dynamics in neurofluid disorders, but their reliability depends on consistent region‐of‐interest (ROI) delineation and postprocessing.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Automated Cerebrospinal Fluid Flow Quantification in Hydrocephalus Using Phase-Contrast Magnetic Resonance Imaging》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Materials and Methods · nbm70431-sec-0002-p1】This section describes the methodological pipeline used to evaluate automatic and manual CSF segmentation at the C2–C3 level in PC‐MRI. First, PC‐MRI data were acquired in hydrocephalus patients and segmented by human operators and the pretrained flow‐aware DL model. This initial acquisition‐and‐segmentation stage is summarized in Figure 1. Next, the resulting binary masks were converted into quantitative measurements by extracting the ROI surface area, background‐corrected flow waveform, peak flow amplitude, and SV, as illustrated in Figure 2. Finally, these geometric and hydrodynamic parameters were compared across operators and against the multi‐expert reference using complementary repeatability and agreement analyses.

【Introduction · nbm70431-sec-0001-p2】The cervical C2–C3 level is a relevant region for quantifying CSF dynamics with PC‐MRI because it captures spinal subarachnoid oscillations that are tightly coupled to intracranial blood‐volume changes over the cardiac cycle, and flow‐derived measures at this level—such as peak flow and SV—have shown good reliability and clinical relevance in studies of craniospinal hydrodynamics [10, 11, 12]. However, quantitative analysis at C2–C3 remains demanding because the cervical subarachnoid space has a complex geometry, flow‐sensitive contrast can be limited, and PC‐MRI measurements are vulnerable to partial‐volume effects, eddy‐current‐related background offsets, slice prescription errors, and other sources of variability that influence ROI delineation and downstream flow estimates [11]. In patients, this task may potentially become more challenging when pathology introduces anatomical narrowing or abnormal hydrodynamic patterns, such as altered craniospinal flow, reduced subarachnoid cross‐sectional area, hyperdynamic profiles, or near‐blocked flow, which can increase local irregularity of the signal to be segmented [13]. Recent work suggests that automation of CSF flow analysis in PC‐MRI can be approached through different strategies. In the cerebral aqueduct, Tsou et al. developed a convolutional neural network (CNN) framework for direct automatic segmentation of the aqueduct ROI and showed that CNN‐derived flow parameters could approach expert‐level measurements [14]. At the cervical level, Huang et al. reported a pipeline for spinal CSF flow quantification at C2 in PC‐MRI, using YOLOv4 [15] for region detection followed by independent component analysis for segmentation rather than a full DL segmentation framework [16]. In current practice, CSF quantification at C2–C3 still commonly relies on manual or semi‐automatic segmentation [7, 11, 17]. Existing automation studies have addressed CSF flow analysis in other anatomical regions or with different segmentation strategies, whereas direct DL‐based segmentation at C2–C3 remains insufficiently evaluated.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:

【Results · nbm70431-sec-0007-p1】All 10 samples were validated and included in the analysis. Manual segmentation with the semi‐automatic workflow required approximately 1–3 min per delineation, whereas the DL model produced one segmentation per subject in less than 1 s. Table 1 summarizes the quantitative results reported in this section.

【Conclusion · nbm70431-sec-0013-p1】This study showed that a flow‐aware DL model can provide fast, deterministic CSF segmentation with small cohort‐level differences in flow‐derived measurements. Agreement with the flow‐derived multi‐expert reference was lower at the individual level, although this reference was not an independent ground truth, and human segmentations were obtained using the same semi‐automatic flow workflow. The results support automatic segmentation as a practical approach to reduce operator‐dependent variability, whereas broader validation remains necessary.

sections.title: 图表阅读

【FIGURE 1 · nbm70431-fig-0001】FIGURE 1 MRI acquisition and segmentation. Phase‐contrast MRI was acquired at the C2–C3 level. Human segmentation masks were obtained using the semi‐automatic flow software, and the DL model processed centrally cropped 80 × 80‐pixel images.

【FIGURE 2 · nbm70431-fig-0002】FIGURE 2 Parameter extraction. Red contours delineate the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) region of interest at C2–C3 on the magnitude and phase images (32 cardiac frames each). Segmentation masks and background‐corrected, phase‐derived velocities were used to obtain the CSF flow waveform. Peak flow amplitude (Amp) is the difference between maximum and minimum flow, indicated by the purple arrow. Stroke volume (SV) is the integral of absolute flow over the cardiac cycle, represented by the total shaded area above and below zero.

【FIGURE 4 · nbm70431-fig-0004】FIGURE 4 Bland–Altman analysis of agreement with the multi‐expert reference. Agreement of the novice operator, Expert 1 and DL model with the multi‐expert reference values for region‐of‐interest surface area, peak flow amplitude, and stroke volume. For the novice operator and Expert 1, both sessions were averaged. Annotated p‐values assess whether the mean method‐minus‐reference difference differs from zero using two‐sided one‐sample t‐tests on the 10 patient‐level differences, with Holm correction across the nine panels. No mean bias was statistically significant after correction at α = 0.05. The solid horizontal lines indicate mean differences, and the dashed lines indicate the 95% limits of agreement.
